name: The four passions (kaṣāya)
description: Anger, pride, deceit and greed — the glue that makes karma stick to the soul — each in four grades from endless-binding to smouldering; their conquest is liberation (YŚ 4.5).
antidotes: forbearance, humility, straightforwardness, contentment (the first four of the ten virtues)

equivalents.note: Overlapping lists of passions; the Jain four include pride and deceit.

name: The nine quasi-passions (nokaṣāya)
description: Laughter, liking, disliking, grief, fear, disgust and the three sexual drives, which accompany the passions (TS 8.9).

name: Wrong view (mithyātva)
description: Belief contrary to the realities, the first and root cause of bondage; five kinds (one-sided, contrary, indiscriminate reverence, doubt, ignorance — Digambara list) or innate and acquired.
antidotes: right view through the three processes and the breaking of the knot

name: The five causes of bondage
description: Wrong view, non-abstinence, carelessness, passion and activity (TS 8.1).

name: Non-abstinence (avirati)
description: Not having renounced violence and the other sins — the second cause of bondage, removed by the vows.

equivalents.note: YS 1.30 avirati is craving for sense objects.

name: Carelessness (pramāda)
description: Heedlessness in conduct — gossip, passions, indulgence of the senses, sleep, affection — which makes an injury 'violence' (TS 7.13, 8.1).

equivalents.note: YS 1.30 pramāda is neglect of the means to samādhi.

name: The five sins
description: Violence, falsehood, stealing, unchastity and possessiveness, from which the vows abstain (TS 7.1, 7.13–17).

name: The three thorns (śalya)
description: Deceit, longing for future reward and wrong view, which disqualify a vow-holder (TS 7.18).

name: Nidāna (binding wish for reward)
description: Wishing that one's austerities bring worldly or heavenly reward — a thorn, a sorrowful meditation and a fault of the final fast (TS 7.37, 9.33).

name: Transgressions of right view
description: Doubt, desire, disgust, praise of wrong-believers and intimacy with them (TS 7.23).

name: Transgressions of the vows
description: Five partial lapses for each vow and virtue (TS 7.24–37), e.g. binding, beating, mutilating, overloading and starving for non-violence.

name: The three follies (mūḍhatā)
description: Folly regarding the world (bathing in rivers, heaping stones for merit), regarding gods (worshipping passionate deities for favours) and regarding false ascetics — faults of right view (Ratnakaraṇḍa).

name: The eight prides (mada)
description: Pride in knowledge, honour, family, caste, power, wealth, austerity and body, which spoil right view (Ratnakaraṇḍa); self-praise binds low status (TS 6.25).

name: The four kinds of idle talk (vikathā)
description: Talk about women, food, country and kings — forms of carelessness to be avoided by ascetics.

name: The four instincts (saṃjñā)
description: The craving for food, fear, sexual desire and possessiveness found in all worldly beings.

name: Sorrowful and cruel meditation
description: Brooding on the disagreeable, the agreeable, pain and future reward (ārta), and delighting in violence, falsehood, theft and guarding possessions (raudra); they cause bondage and bad rebirth (TS 9.28–35).

name: Evil meditation (asad-dhyāna)
description: Meditation and mantra used to harm, attract, subjugate or kill others, or meditation on passionate and fearsome forms (Jñānārṇava; YŚ 9).

name: Haribhadra's eight faults of the mind in yoga
description: Fatigue, anxiety, distraction, agitation, confusion, delight in other things, pain and attachment, removed one by one through the eight views (YDS 16).

equivalents.note: Both are lists of obstacles to yoga; the items differ.

name: One-sided dogmatism (ekānta)
description: Holding one aspect or standpoint as the whole truth — the root of rival doctrines and of sectarian quarrel; the Adhyātma critics apply it also to one-sided niścaya and one-sided vyavahāra (Āptamīmāṃsā; Jñānasāra 16; Mokṣamārga Prakāśaka).

name: Conformity to the crowd (loka-saṃjñā)
description: Following what people do and approve instead of the truth; Yaśovijaya devotes an aṣṭaka of the Jñānasāra to renouncing it.

name: Hypocrisy (dambha)
description: Religious practice for show; its renunciation is the first step of adhyātma (Adhyātmasāra).

name: Poison and venom performance
description: Religious acts done for this-worldly gain ('poison') or heavenly reward ('venom'), and mechanical performance, which do not lead to liberation (Yogabindu).

name: Identifying the self with the body
description: The outer self's error of taking the body and external things as oneself (Samādhitantra 5), overcome by discriminative knowledge.

name: The destructive karmas
description: Knowledge-obscuring, perception-obscuring, deluding and obstructive karma, which veil the soul's own qualities; their destruction yields omniscience (TS 10.1).

name: Attachment to powers
description: Seeking or displaying supernatural attainments — entering other bodies, powers from breath-control — which distract from liberation (YŚ 6.1; Jñānārṇava).

name: The twenty-two hardships
description: Hunger, thirst, cold, heat and the other afflictions that may make an ascetic swerve from the path unless endured (TS 9.8–9).

name: The three inauspicious soul-colourings
description: Black, blue and grey leśyās, the colouring of cruel and sorrowful states (TS 3.3; Gommaṭasāra).
